content: When applying insecticides to vegetation around houses to create a barrier zone, the droplet size produced by mist blowers should ideally range between 50–100 µm VMD. This size minimizes the rapid fallout of larger droplets from the airflow. The output through a nozzle depends on the design of the sprayer and must be specified according to the type of application and the equipment to which the nozzle is fitted. If the equipment is powered by a gasoline engine or other motorized systems, ear protectors must be provided and used if the noise level at the operator’s ear exceeds 85 decibels. The requirement for ear protection should be permanently marked on the equipment and included in the operating manual. Noise levels should be measured using a Sound Level Meter that complies with IEC 61672-1:2002 or equivalent standards. The equipment must have clear markings that allow the operator to easily locate and identify the manufacturer’s name, contact details, machine type, date of manufacture or serial number, and the position of key components affecting routine use. The positions of valves or switches indicating on/off positions, nozzle size, flow restrictors, and other controls must be clearly visible. The type of liquid to be added to any tank must also be clearly marked, and these markings must remain legible despite exposure to pesticide formulations or solvents. Pesticide application equipment must be accompanied by a clear, simple, and illustrated user manual. This manual should detail the method of operation, including calibration, safety precautions, maintenance procedures, and essential spare parts required for routine maintenance. The manual should also provide information on safe handling of undiluted pesticides, mixing chemicals, filling the tank, disposal of leftover spray liquid and empty containers, nozzle sizes and types, flow rates, spray quality, operating pressures, and precautions to minimize operator and environmental exposure to pesticides. Users of vector control equipment should maintain a record of its use on an individual Sprayer History card, including dates of maintenance and spare parts used. New types and brands of equipment require field evaluation following initial laboratory testing. Compression sprayers are primarily used for residual spraying of wall surfaces and applying larvicides. These sprayers consist of a cylindrical tank equipped with a hand-operated air pump, a pressure-release safety device, a hose connected to a dip-tube, a shoulder strap, a footrest for stability during pressurization, a trigger valve with a locking-off device, a straight lance, a control flow valve (CFV), and a nozzle. The air pump must be capable of pressurizing the tank to the recommended maximum operational pressure with no more than 60 full strokes. The pump cylinder must withstand internal and external pressures up to twice the maximum operating pressure of the spray tank. The pump handle should be at least 200 mm long for comfortable two-handed operation. A pressure release device must be fitted to the top of the sprayer to completely depressurize the tank before opening the lid. The valve should reseal when the lid is refitted to allow normal operation without leakage. A pressure relief valve may also be included to prevent pressurization beyond the manufacturer’s prescribed limits. The trigger valve must have a positive lock-off position, and its lever should be at least 100 mm long. Filters in the trigger valve must have a smaller mesh size than the nozzle aperture and should be easily accessible for frequent cleaning. The lance attached to the trigger valve should be at least 500 mm long and fitted with a control flow valve to ensure a constant flow rate as the tank pressure decreases. Knapsack sprayers, typically lever-operated, are mainly used for spraying larvicides and are not suitable for indoor residual spraying. These sprayers consist of a knapsack tank with two shoulder straps and a waist strap, a manually operated pump, a hose connecting the pump output to a lance, and a lance with a trigger valve, control flow valve, and nozzle. The pump can be either diaphragm or piston type, operated manually by a lever designed for rightor left-handed use. The lever should be at least 400 mm long and operate within a 400 mm arc of movement. The pump should deliver >70 L/h of liquid with 20–30 lever strokes per minute, maintaining pressure deviations within ±10%. Motorized knapsack mist blowers are used for rapid treatment of open water bodies for larval control and for barrier treatments on house eaves and foliage to reduce mosquito entry. These sprayers have an engine-driven fan that produces a high-velocity airstream into which the pesticide liquid is metered and projected at least 10 m upwards into trees. The engine, mounted on a knapsack frame, must have an easy-start mechanism, a fuel tank below the engine, and guards for all moving parts and the exhaust to prevent injury. Engine controls, including a stop switch and speed control, must be visible in front of the operator during use. The engine mounting must dampen vibrations, and all regulated parts must be permanently marked for identification. The fuel tank capacity should allow at least one hour of field operation without stopping, with fuel consumption below 2 L/h at optimum engine speed. The type of fuel and fuel mix must be permanently indicated on the fuel tank or machine. The knapsack frame should have a padded backrest to rest comfortably on the operator’s back, and the straps should be adjustable, padded, and at least 75 cm long with a width of 50 ± 5 mm. Nozzles must comply with international standards, such as ISO 10625:2005, and their flow rates and spray patterns should be regularly checked for consistency. The choice of nozzle depends on the area being treated, with straight jet nozzles used for projecting spray further and flat fan or cone nozzles for wider coverage.
